definition: to voluntarily give up or stop claiming something
memoryTip: Re-LINQUISH: let go of a claim or hold (think relinquish the crown).
correctPassage: After the merger, the founder agreed to relinquish day-to-day control of the company.
wrongPassages: Investors hoped to relinquish a larger share of the market through aggressive pricing.
She relinquished the scholarship by studying harder and raising her average.
The brief was so relinquish that jurors needed almost no further testimony.

definition: to confirm or support as true; to give a personal guarantee
memoryTip: VOUCH for a friend: put your word behind their honesty.
correctPassage: Two former supervisors will vouch for his reliability on the job.
wrongPassages: Several experts plan to vouch the methodology as too flawed for publication.
The editor tried to vouch the controversial findings by cutting the final section.
Analysts worked to vouch public opinion through a lengthy nationwide survey.

definition: providing additional help; serving as a secondary support
memoryTip: AUX jack: the extra, secondary connection that helps out.
correctPassage: The hospital kept an auxiliary power system ready in case the main grid failed.
wrongPassages: The auxiliary engine alone powered the entire vessel; no other motors were installed.
Please auxiliary the fragile samples before shipping them overseas.
Critics called the initiative auxiliary and therefore the project's sole priority.

definition: to lead an attack, campaign, or major effort
memoryTip: Tip of the SPEAR: you go first and lead the charge.
correctPassage: A small committee will spearhead fundraising for the new library wing.
wrongPassages: He agreed to spearhead the initiative only after every other department had finished its work.
Lobbyists worked to spearhead the reform bill by filing endless procedural delays.
Reviewers found the conclusion spearhead and unsupported by any of the data.

definition: to draw out a response, fact, or reaction
memoryTip: E-LICIT draws it out—don't confuse with illicit (illegal).
correctPassage: The interviewer's silence helped elicit a more candid answer from the witness.
wrongPassages: City council voted to elicit overnight parking near the transit station.
Officials rewrote the policy to elicit dissent before it could reach the press.
Alumni were asked to elicit funds for the new scholarship endowment.
